name: Mongolian Ground Beef
why: You named this as one of the three dinners worth having back, on 2026-08-14. The version that was here before was written by an agent and tuned to whatever was in the cupboard: white sugar, honey and oyster sauce standing in for a sauce nobody had cooked. This one is Salt and Lavender's recipe instead, unchanged, at her scale. Four ingredients in the sauce, one pan, and the beef does not need slicing because it is already ground.

serves.proteinMath: ESTIMATE, and it is the one number here nobody has read off a label. 1 pound of lean ground beef is 454 g. Lean ground beef is about 20 g of protein per 100 g raw, so 454 g is about 91 g, and across her 4 servings that is about 23 g a bowl. THE 20 g/100 g IS A GENERIC FIGURE, not the Pre Pak label, which has not been photographed. Weigh and read the label before trusting this to a daily total. Rice adds more and is not counted here, because the source gives no rice amount and none has been invented.

ingredients.prep: 1 pound. On the digital scale that is 454 g. Your freezer bags are 500 g and 250 g, so one 500 g bag is 46 g more than she asks for
cut into 1 inch pieces. Only the green parts go in this dish, so the white ends are spare
packed, meaning pressed down into the cup rather than spooned in loose

steps.text: Add the beef to a skillet over medium-high heat. Cook until browned, breaking it up with your spoon as it cooks (about 8-10 minutes). Spoon out excess fat as needed.
steps.sourceText: Add the beef to a skillet over medium-high heat. Cook until browned, breaking it up with your spoon as it cooks (about 8-10 minutes). Spoon out excess fat as needed.

heat.target: Hot enough that the beef hisses steadily the whole time it is in the pan. If it goes quiet it is stewing in its own liquid instead of browning, so bring it up until the hiss comes back.
heat.recheck: About a minute after the beef goes in, once its water has come out.

doneness.test: Push a clump against the side of the pan to break it open and look at the cut face. Browned is no red and no pink left anywhere in it.

steps.look:
SKILLET means a frying pan, and yours is the large STAINLESS one rather than the non-stick. Browning is the one job stainless is better at, and nothing in this dish has to be released in one piece.

BREAKING IT UP means pressing the lump apart with the edge of the spoon as it cooks, so it ends as loose crumbles rather than one grey patty. Keep at it every half minute or so for the whole 8 to 10 minutes.

SPOON OUT EXCESS FAT is her phrase and she gives no amount, so here is the amount: tilt the pan so the liquid fat runs to the low side and lift out anything that pools there, into a jar and not down the sink. Lean beef may give almost none. Leaving it in makes the sauce greasy rather than glossy.

The 8 to 10 minutes is her number. The doneness test above is what actually decides it.

steps.text: Meanwhile, add the sauce ingredients to a bowl and whisk together.
steps.sourceText: Meanwhile, add the sauce ingredients to a bowl and whisk together.
steps.look:
MEANWHILE means while the beef is browning. If that feels like two things at once, take the pan off the heat and make the sauce first. Nothing here is harmed by waiting, and her order is a convenience rather than a requirement.

THE SAUCE INGREDIENTS are the seven on the list above that are not the beef and not the scallions. They all go into one bowl together.

WHISK TOGETHER until you cannot see any cornstarch settled on the bottom. Cornstarch sinks, so lift the bowl and look underneath before you stop. Any left behind will not thicken anything.

The cornstarch is what makes the sauce turn glossy and cling instead of running off. It has to go into cold liquid like this. Tipped straight into a hot pan it turns into lumps.

steps.text: Add the scallions to the skillet and also pour the sauce in. Cook for another couple of minutes until the sauce thickens up.
steps.sourceText: Add the scallions to the skillet and also pour the sauce in. Cook for another couple of minutes until the sauce thickens up.

heat.target: Bubbling steadily across the whole surface, not just at the edge. The sauce has to actually boil for the cornstarch to thicken it.
heat.recheck: Straight after the sauce goes in. Cold sauce drops the pan temperature, so it may go quiet for a moment before it comes back.

doneness.test: Her endpoint is the sauce thickening up. Drag the spoon through it and watch the bare metal it leaves behind: while it is thin the sauce floods back instantly, and when it has thickened the gap stays open for about a second.

steps.look:
WHISK THE SAUCE AGAIN right before it goes in. It will have separated in the couple of minutes it sat there and the cornstarch will be back on the bottom of the bowl.

The scallions and the sauce go in together, which is her order.

A COUPLE OF MINUTES is her time. The spoon test above is what decides, because how fast it thickens depends on how hot the pan is.

steps.text: If needed, season with salt & pepper to taste. Serve over rice or noodles.
steps.sourceText: If needed, season with salt & pepper to taste. Serve over rice or noodles.
steps.look:
TASTE IT FIRST, before adding anything. A third of a cup of soy sauce is already a lot of salt and it may well need none, which is why she wrote IF NEEDED.

This app normally refuses to write “to taste”, because it means nothing to someone still learning. Here it is her sentence, so it stays, and this is what it means: take a spoonful, eat it, and only reach for the salt if it tastes flat.

RICE OR NOODLES is her choice to offer and yours to make. For rice: the rice cooker takes cupfuls of its own cup, with water to the matching line on the pot, and no other measurement is involved. Start it before step 1 and it lands when the beef does.

Nothing in this recipe gives a rice amount, so none has been invented, and the protein figure counts the beef only.

provenance.statement: Every instruction is Salt and Lavender's own sentence, in her order, with her times and her amounts, at her scale of 4 servings. Nothing was scaled, substituted, re-panned or re-timed. What this app adds is the layer a printed page cannot: which of his pans she means, what a word means, an observable for the induction hob where she writes medium-high, a test for the endpoint she names, and the protein arithmetic. All of it renders as visibly separate from her sentences. The previous version of this dish was agent-written, used white sugar, honey and oyster sauce because those were in the cupboard, and had never been cooked.

sources.name: Salt & Lavender
